X.C. Power-Off Stalls
Introduction
How
Aerodynamics 											AI.X.C.K2
A stall occurs when the smooth airflow over the wing is disrupted, and lift decreases rapidly
This happens when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack (AOA)
The critical AOA varies with aircraft, but is usually around 15-20o in GA aircraft
The Critical Angle of Attack/CLMAX (picture below)
The point at which the airflow separates and there is a rapid reduction in lift is the stalling angle of attack, or the critical angle of attack, or CLMAX (the Maximum Coefficient of Lift)
CL (Coefficient of Lift)
Measurement of lift as it relates to AOA
Determined by wind tunnel tests; based on airfoil design/AOA
Any AOA beyond CLMAX results in a stall and lift drops off rapidly
Stall Characteristics
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall at the wing root and progress out to the wing tips
Aileron effectiveness is maintained at the wingtips, maintaining control
Various designs can be used to accomplish this:
Twisting the wing to create a lower angle of attack at the wing tip compared to the wing root
Adding strips to the first 20-25% of the leading edge to induce a stall earlier than otherwise
There’s More than One Way to Exceed the Critical AOA
If at ANY time the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Low Speed
As airspeed decreases, the AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
At a slow enough speed, the critical AOA is exceeded
High Speed
If an aircraft is in a high-speed dive and the pilot pulls back sharply on the elevator
Although the nose is raised, the aircraft continues downward for some amount of time
AOA changes from low to very high while the flight path remains the same
The aircraft reaches the critical AOA at a speed much higher than the published stall speed
Turns
The stall speed of an aircraft is higher in a level turn than in straight-and-level flight
In turn, AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
If during the turn the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Various Factors & their Effect on Stall Speed 						AI.X.C.K2
A stall can occur at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting, depending on the total factors affecting the aircraft
Airspeed & Power Settings
Low Speed and/or Low Power Setting
Same as above
High Speed and/or High-Power Setting
Same as above
Additionally, in low wing planes, high power settings may reduce stall speed and increase lift
Propeller airflow over the wing roots can provide some lift even if the wing is stalled
Yaw Effects
Increased power at slow airspeeds and high angles of attack results in increased left turning tendencies – Anticipate considerable right rudder to maintain coordination
Torque Reaction – Based on Newton’s 3rd Law
The engine parts/propeller rotate right, an equal force attempts to rotate the plane left
In Flight: Left rolling tendency
On the Ground: Left turning tendency
Corrected by offsetting the engine, aileron trim tabs, and/or aileron and rudder use
Corkscrew/Slipstream Effect
Corkscrewing propeller air strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer - pushes nose left
Strongest at high prop speeds/low forward speeds
Gyroscopic Action
Precession - Any force takes effect 90o ahead of, and in the direction of rotation
Pitch results in a yawing moment and vice versa
Correct with rudder/elevator
Asymmetric Loading (P Factor)
At high AOAs, the bite of the down moving blade is greater than the up moving blade
Center of thrust moves to the right of the propeller disc, causing a yaw to the left
Correct with right rudder
Configuration (Gear and Flaps)
Flaps - Reduce the stall speed of an aircraft
Most flaps increase the camber of the wing and change the chord line, producing more lift
Note the differing speeds on the airspeed indicator (green arc vs white arc)
Gear
The effects of gear can vary based on the aircraft design and characteristics
Gear extension increases drag and if not properly compensated for could lead to a stall
Weight - As the weight of the aircraft increases, the stall speed increases
The greater the weight, the greater the lift required, and therefore the higher AOA
Closer to the critical AOA
A lighter aircraft will stall at a slower airspeed (opposite of a heavy aircraft)
Center of Gravity (CG)
Forward CG
“Heavier” and consequently slower
More nose-up elevator is required to maintain altitude
Tail must produce a greater down load resulting in greater wing loading
Added wing loading requires increased lift to maintain altitude
Higher Stall Speed
Higher AOA results in more induced drag and a higher stall speed (like heavy aircraft)
More Controllable in a Stall/Spin
More controllable than aft loaded aircraft
Due to the longer arm from elevator to CG
And the farther forward the CG, the greater the tendency for the nose to pitch down
Aft Loaded Aircraft
“Lighter” and consequently faster
Less nose-up pressure required
Lower nose requires less down load
Decreased down load reduces wing loading, decreasing lift required to maintain altitude
Lower Stall Speed
Lower AOA results in less induced drag allowing for a faster cruise speed & lower stall speed
Less Controllable in a Stall/Spin
Recovery from a stall becomes progressively more difficult as the CG moves aft
Shortens the arm from CG to the elevator
Additionally, the farther aft the CG, the less tendency for the nose to pitch down on its own
Load Factor
Any increase in the load factor increases the stall speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Pulling out of a steep descent, steep turns, aggressive control inputs, etc.
Bank Angle & Load Factor
Increased load factors are a characteristic of all banked turns
Tremendous loads are imposed on an airplane at bank angles above 45o
Snow, Ice, & Frost
Increase the stall speed
Disrupt smooth airflow over the wing causing the boundary layer to separate at an AOA lower than the critical AOA
To make matters worse, as ice accumulates weight is increased
More lift is required due to the added weight, but less lift is available due to the ice
As little as .8 millimeters of ice on the upper wing increases drag and reduces lift by 25%
RM: Power-Off Stall Situations 							AI.X.C.K4, AI.X.C.R1
Generally, associated with approach to landing conditions and configurations
Attempting to recover from a high sink rate on final approach using only an increased pitch attitude
Improper airspeed control on final approach and other segments of the traffic pattern
Distractions, disorientation, windshear, poor region of reversed command understanding/control, etc.
RM: Stall Warning Range & Limitations 		 					AI.X.C.R2
Buffet: Tends to occur prior to the stall horn
May not always occur (Ex: Cross controlled stalls can occur with little to no warning)
Stall Horn: Designed to provide warning of an approaching stall and time for stall recovery
Per 23.207
Must be a clear & distinct stall warning with flaps and gear in any normal position
Warning must begin at least 5 knots above stall speed and continue until the stall occurs
Must provide the pilot time to take action to avert the stall
Operational Ranges & Limitations: Vary between aircraft
Reference the POH for specific info (ex. Uncoordinated flight may inhibit airflow at the indicator)
Power-Off Stalls 										AI.X.C.K1
Entry
Pre-Maneuver Checklist; Clear the area
Select an altitude - Must recover prior to 1,500’ AGL
Landing configuration
Note the heading (bug the heading)
Getting into the Straight Stall
Slow to normal approach speed while maintaining altitude
Configure for landing
Visually - Find a reference off the nose to maintain direction and to assist with pitch attitude
Smoothly lower the nose to the normal approach attitude and maintain approach speed
Once stable, reduce power to idle and smoothly raise the nose to an attitude that will induce a stall
Simulate a flare to landing
Just like in slow flight, use smooth movements in controlling the airplane, nothing jerky
Getting into the Turning Stall
Same procedures as a straight-ahead stall, except a specific bank angle is maintained
When the power is set and the descent established, establish the desired bank angle
Aileron pressure must be continually adjusted to keep the bank constant (Overbanking tendency)
Maintain coordination
Increase control pressure as the aircraft slows and controls become less effective
Recognizing the Stall 										AI.X.C.K3
Announce the stages of the stall: Stall Warning Horn, Reduced Control Effectiveness, Buffet, Stall
Sight: Attitude of the plane
Sound: Stall warning horn, reduced RPM, slowing airspeed / airflow
Feel: Mushy/less effective controls, leaning back, buffeting and vibrations just before stall
Kinesthesia (sensing of movements by feel, “seat of the pants,” your “spidey sense,” sinking feeling)
Experience based – Developed properly, you can recognize when something doesn’t feel right
Aircraft Specific: Note any aircraft specific designs, indicators, characteristics, etc.
RM: Recovery (RM: Stall recovery procedure)					AI.X.C.K5, AI.X.C.R4
Basics: Disconnect, Pitch, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize, Configure (perform each step as appropriate)
Disconnect the autopilot
Pitch nose-down – AOA must be decreased positively and immediately
Trim nose-down, if required
Roll wings level – Regain / maintain directional control with coordinated aileron and rudder
Reorients the lift vector vertical for a more effective recovery and climb
Do not attempt to level the wings prior to reducing angle of attack (can aggravate stall)
Thrust/power as necessary - Stalls can occur at high/low power & airspeeds, adjust as required
Generally, in a power-off stall, maximum allowable power should be applied
Right rudder will be required to maintain coordination/heading
Stabilize/establish the desired flight path - Go around and climb at the desired airspeed VY (VX)
Configure – Once in a climb, configure as required (same flap and gear retraction as a go around)
Ailerons & Recovery
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall progressively outward from the wing root
Aileron control is maintained at high AOAs, providing more stable stall characteristics
During recovery, the return of lift begins at the tips and progresses towards the roots
Ailerons can be used to level the wings
If the wing is fully stalled (ailerons included), using ailerons can aggravate the stall
Attempting to raise the low (stalled) wing increases its AOA, further stalling the wing
Rudder and Recovery
Primary cause of spins is exceeding the critical AOA with improper rudder (uncoordinated flight)
Maintaining directional control/coordinated flight with rudder is vital in avoiding a spin
Common Errors (AFH 5-21)									AI.X.C.K6
Failure to adequately clear the area
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery
Inability to recognize an impending stall condition
Failure to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls, or recovering too early on a full stall
Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls
Failure to maintain proper coordination with the rudder throughout the stall and recovery
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped, prior to reducing AOA
Recovery is attempted without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA
Excessive forward pressure and/or not holding nose down controls until the stall warning is eliminated
Pilot attempts to level the wings and/or recover with power before reducing AOA
Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated
Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on entry, & inadvertent secondary stall during recovery
Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery
Losing situational awareness and failing to return to desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions
RM: Hazards
Stall Warning during Normal Operation 							AI.X.C.R3
Recover
The first thought is not how or why this is happening, the first thought is to recover/fix the problem
When safe, then you can figure out how it happened
Secondary Stalls 										AI.X.C.R5
Occurs after recovery from a preceding stall
Pilot does not sufficiently reduce AOA or attempts to recover using only pitch or power
Perform the stall recovery procedure again, but do it right
Mitigation: Practice & perform proper recovery procedures (Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize)
Accelerated Stalls 										AI.X.C.R5
Higher G loads increase the stall speed (Ex. Steep turns, aggressive pull up)
Recover at the first indication of a stall: Push, roll, thrust, stabilize
Often, just removing the back pressure will break the stall
Mitigation: Use smooth control pressures
Cross-Controlled Stalls 									AI.X.C.R5
Aileron and rudder in opposite directions can lead to a cross-controlled stall
May have little to no warning of the impending stall
Release the crossed-controls and recover: Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Mitigation: Maintain coordination
Environmental Elements 								 	AI.X.C.R6
Turbulence
Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs to maintain altitude can exceed the critical AOA
In moderate/severe turbulence/strong crosswinds, use a higher-than-normal approach speed
When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence & speed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall
Microbursts
Can induce wind speeds greater than 100 knots and downdrafts as strong as 6,000 fpm
Depending on strength, climb ability can be minimized, if not eliminated
Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact
Can quickly lead to a stall making the problem far worse than it already is
If ground contact becomes a concern, increase pitch to minimize sink while avoiding a stall
Do not fly in or around thunderstorms or heavy rain showers where microbursts are most common
The best risk mitigation starts with effective planning
In the case of a microburst follow the POH procedures
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
See Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for details on recognizing/avoiding microbursts, and strategies for escape
High Density Altitude
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Collision Hazards 										AI.X.C.R7
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program

Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules

Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons/property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Antenna Towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally from the structure
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.

Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Sterile cockpit procedures
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition

Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)

“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there

Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

paragraphs.text: X.D. Power-On Stalls
Introduction
How
Stall Aerodynamics 										AI.X.D.K2
A stall occurs when the smooth airflow over the wing is disrupted, and lift decreases rapidly
This happens when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack (AOA)
The critical AOA varies with aircraft, but is usually around 15-20o in GA aircraft
The Critical Angle of Attack/CLMAX (picture below)
The point at which the airflow separates and there is a rapid reduction in lift is the stalling angle of attack, or the critical angle of attack, or CLMAX (Maximum Coefficient of Lift)
CL (Coefficient of Lift)
Measurement of lift as it relates to AOA
Determined by wind tunnel tests; based on airfoil design/AOA
Any AOA beyond CLMAX results in a stall and lift drops off rapidly
Stall Characteristics
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall at the wing root and progress out to the wing tips
Aileron effectiveness is maintained at the wingtips, maintaining control
Various designs can be used to accomplish this:
Twisting the wing to create a lower angle of attack at the wing tip compared to the wing root
Adding strips to the first 20-25% of the leading edge to induce a stall earlier than otherwise
There’s More than One Way to Exceed the Critical AOA
If at ANY time the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Low Speed
As airspeed decreases, the AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
At a slow enough speed, the critical AOA is exceeded
High Speed
If an aircraft is in a high-speed dive and the pilot pulls back sharply on the elevator
Although the nose is raised, the aircraft continues downward for some amount of time
AOA changes from low to very high while the flight path remains the same
The aircraft reaches the critical AOA at a speed much higher than the published stall speed
Turns
The stall speed of an aircraft is higher in a level turn than in straight-and-level flight
In a turn, AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
If during the turn the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Various Factors and their Effect on Stall Speed 					AI.X.D.K2
A stall can occur at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting, depending on the total factors affecting the aircraft
Airspeed & Power Settings
Low Speed and/or Low Power Setting
Same as above
High Speed and/or High-Power Setting
Same as above
Additionally, in low wing planes, high power settings may reduce stall speed and increase lift
Propeller airflow over the wing roots can provide some lift even if the wing is stalled
Yaw Effects
Increased power at slow airspeeds and high angles of attack results in increased left turning tendencies - Anticipate considerable right rudder to maintain coordination
Torque Reaction – Based on Newton’s 3rd Law
The engine parts/propeller rotate right, an equal force attempts to rotate the plane left
In Flight: Left rolling tendency
On the Ground: Left turning  tendency
Corrected by offsetting the engine, aileron trim tabs, and/or aileron and rudder use
Corkscrew/Slipstream Effect
Corkscrewing propeller air strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer - pushes nose left
Strongest at high prop speeds/low forward speeds
Gyroscopic Action
Precession - Any force takes effect 90o ahead of, and in the direction of rotation
Pitch results in a yawing moment and vice versa
Correct with rudder/elevator
Asymmetric Loading (P Factor)
At high AOAs, the bite of the down moving blade is greater than the up moving blade
The center of thrust moves to the right of the propeller disc, causing a yaw to the left
Correct with right rudder
Configuration (Gear & Flaps)
Flaps - Reduce the stall speed of an aircraft
Most flaps increase the camber of the wing and change the chord line, producing more lift
Note the differing speeds on the airspeed indicator (green arc vs white arc)
Gear
The effects of gear can vary based on the aircraft design and characteristics
Gear extension increases drag and if not properly compensated for could lead to a stall
Weight - As the weight of the aircraft increases, the stall speed increases
The greater the weight, the greater the lift required, and therefore the higher AOA
Closer to the critical angle of attack
A lighter aircraft will stall at a slower airspeed (opposite of a heavy aircraft)
Center of Gravity
Forward CG
“Heavier,” and consequently slower
More nose-up elevator is required to maintain altitude
Tail must produce a greater down load resulting in greater wing loading
Added wing loading requires increased lift to maintain altitude
Higher Stall Speed
Higher AOA results in more induced drag and a higher stall speed (like heavy aircraft)
More Controllable in a Stall/Spin
More controllable than aft loaded aircraft
Due to the longer arm from elevator to CG
Additionally, the farther forward the CG, the greater the tendency for the nose to pitch down
Aft Loaded Aircraft
“Lighter,” and consequently faster
Less nose-up pressure required
Lower nose requires less down load
Decreased down load reduces wing loading, decreasing lift required to maintain altitude
Lower Stall Speed
Lower AOA results in less induced drag allowing for a faster cruise speed & lower stall speed
Less Controllable in a Stall/Spin
Recovery from a stall becomes progressively more difficult as the CG moves aft
The arm from the CG to the elevator is shortened
Additionally, the farther aft the CG, the less tendency for the nose to pitch down on its own
Load Factor
Any increase in the load factor increases the stall speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Pulling out of a steep descent, steep turns, aggressive control inputs, etc.
Bank Angle & Load Factor
Increased load factors are a characteristic of all banked turns
Tremendous loads are imposed on an airplane at bank angles above 45o
Snow, Ice, & Frost
Increase the stall speed
Disrupt smooth airflow over the wing causing the boundary layer to separate at an AOA lower than the critical AOA
To make matters worse, as ice accumulates weight is increased
More lift is required due to the added weight, but less lift is available due to the ice
As little as .8 millimeters of ice on the upper wing increases drag and reduces lift by 25%
RM: Power-On Stall Situations 							AI.X.D.K4, AI.X.D.R1
High power, high pitch situations
Generally associated with takeoff, climb & go-arounds. Most hazardous of these situations are likely:
Short field takeoff – high pitch, VX climb – closer to the stall speed
Go Around – changing configuration, pitch, power. Significant nose up trim, and distractions
Improper airspeed control in high power, high pitch, or similar situations
RM: Stall Warning Range & Limitations 		 					AI.X.D.R2
Buffet: Tends to occur prior to the stall horn
May not always occur (Ex: Cross controlled stalls can occur with little to no warning)
Stall Horn: Designed to provide warning of an approaching stall and time for stall recovery
Must be a clear & distinct stall warning with flaps and gear in any normal position
Warning must begin at least 5 knots above stall speed and continue until the stall occurs
Must provide the pilot time to take action to avert the stall
Operational Ranges & Limitations: Vary between aircraft
Reference the POH for specific information
Ex: Uncoordinated flight may inhibit airflow at the indicator
Power-On Stalls 										AI.X.D.K1
Differences: Considerably louder and steeper than a power-off stall
Entry
Pre-Maneuver Checklist; Clear the area
Select an altitude - Must recover prior to 1,500’ AGL
Takeoff configuration (can be practiced clean as well)
Note the heading (bug the heading)
Getting into the Straight-Ahead Stall
Reduce power to slow to normal lift off speed while maintaining altitude
Visually - Nose pitches above the horizon; use a cloud, or other high visual reference
At VR, increase to takeoff power and maintain the specified climb attitude
Counter left turning tendencies with right rudder
As speed decreases & controls lose effectiveness, increase back pressure and right rudder
Visual references are primary, but back them up with the instruments
Use smooth movements to control the aircraft, nothing jerky
Getting into the Turning Stall
Same as a straight stall, except a specific bank is maintained (15-20o - Airplane Flying Handbook)
Apply power & pitch for the climb, and then establish the desired bank angle
Continually adjust aileron pressure to maintain bank
Reduced airspeed / control effectiveness
Overbanking tendency requires opposite aileron
Maintain coordination
Especially important in a turning, power-on stall due to the increased chance of a spin
Recognizing the Stall 										AI.X.D.K3
Announce the stages of the stall: Stall Warning Horn, Reduced Control Effectiveness, Buffet, Stall
Sight: Nose high attitude (especially high in a power on stall)
Sound: Stall warning horn, reduced RPM due to propeller load, slowing airspeed / airflow
Feel: Mushy / less effective controls, leaning back, buffeting and vibrations just before stall
Kinesthesia (sensing of movements by feel, “seat of the pants,” your “spidey sense”)
Experience based. When properly developed you can recognize when something doesn’t feel right
Aircraft Specific: Note any aircraft specific designs, indicators, characteristics, etc.
RM: Recovery - Disconnect, Pitch, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize, Configure 		AI.X.D.K5, AI.X.D.R4
Perform each step as appropriate
Disconnect the autopilot
Pitch nose down – Pitch attitude must be decreased immediately
Roll wings level – Regain / maintain directional control with coordinated aileron and rudder
Thrust/power as necessary – Stalls can occur at high/low power & airspeeds, adjust as required
In general, in a power-on stall, verify maximum power is set
Stabilize/establish the desired flight path – Establish a climb at the desired airspeed VY (or VX)
Once the stall is broken, do not aggressively lift the nose to reestablish a climb
Use smooth, controlled inputs and monitor the performance to ensure it is ready to climb
Configure – Once in a climb, configure as required (same flap and gear retraction as a go around)
Ailerons and Recovery
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall progressively outward from the wing root
Aileron control is maintained at high AOAs, providing more stable stall characteristics
During recovery, the return of lift begins at the tips and progresses towards the roots
Ailerons can be used to level the wings
If the wing is fully stalled (ailerons included), using ailerons can aggravate the stall
Attempting to raise the low (stalled) wing increases its AOA, further stalling the wing
Rudder and Recovery
The primary cause of spins is exceeding the critical AOA with improper rudder (uncoordinated flight)
Maintaining directional control / coordinated flight with rudder is vital in avoiding a spin
Common Errors (AFH 5-21)									AI.X.D.K6
Failure to adequately clear the area
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery
Inability to recognize an impending stall condition
Failure to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls, or recovering too early on a full stall
Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls
Failure to maintain proper coordination with the rudder throughout the stall and recovery
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped, prior to reducing AOA
Recovery is attempted without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA
Excessive forward pressure or not holding nose down controls until the stall warning is eliminated
Pilot attempts to level the wings and/or recover with power before reducing AOA
Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated
Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on entry, & inadvertent secondary stall during recovery
Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery
Losing situational awareness and failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions
RM: Hazards
Stall Warning during Normal Operation 							AI.X.D.R3
Recover!
The first thought is not how and why is this happening, the first reaction is to recover/fix the problem
When safe, then you can figure out how it happened

Occurs after recovery from a preceding stall
Pilot does not sufficiently reduce AOA or attempts to recover using only pitch or power
Perform the stall recovery procedure again, but do it right
Mitigation: Practice & perform proper recovery procedures (Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize)

Higher G loads increase the stall speed (Ex. Steep turns, aggressive pull up)
Recover at the first indication of a stall
Push, roll, thrust, stabilize
Often, just removing the back pressure will break the stall
Mitigation: Use smooth control pressures
Elevator Trim Stalls 										AI.X.D.R5
Result of adding full power for a go-around with nose-up trim without maintaining control
Recover
Push - Regain control of the pitch attitude
Rough trim the airplane (fine tune later) to remove the excessive nose up pitch
Roll, Thrust, Stabilize as necessary
Once safe/under control, continue the go-around
Preventing Elevator Trim Stalls
Use smooth power applications
Anticipate and overcome the trim forces pitching the nose up, and maintain positive control
Cross-Controlled Stalls 									AI.X.D.R5
Aileron and rudder in opposite directions can lead to a cross-controlled stall
Most common in the traffic pattern
May have little to no warning of the impending stall
Release the crossed-controls and recover: Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Mitigation: Maintain coordination

Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs to maintain altitude can exceed the critical AOA
In moderate/severe turbulence/strong crosswinds, use a higher-than-normal approach speed
When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence & speed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall

Can induce wind speeds greater than 100 knots and downdrafts as strong as 6,000 fpm
Depending on strength, climb ability can be minimized, if not eliminated
Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact
Can quickly lead to a stall making the problem far worse than it already is
If ground contact becomes a concern, increase pitch to minimize sink while avoiding a stall
Do not fly in or around thunderstorms or heavy rain showers where microbursts are most common
The best risk mitigation starts with effective planning
In the case of a microburst follow the POH procedures
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
See Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for details on recognizing/avoiding microbursts, and strategies for escape

They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop

standard_lessons.full_text:
X.D. Power-On Stalls
Introduction
How
Stall Aerodynamics 										AI.X.D.K2
A stall occurs when the smooth airflow over the wing is disrupted, and lift decreases rapidly
This happens when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack (AOA)
The critical AOA varies with aircraft, but is usually around 15-20o in GA aircraft
The Critical Angle of Attack/CLMAX (picture below)
The point at which the airflow separates and there is a rapid reduction in lift is the stalling angle of attack, or the critical angle of attack, or CLMAX (Maximum Coefficient of Lift)
CL (Coefficient of Lift)
Measurement of lift as it relates to AOA
Determined by wind tunnel tests; based on airfoil design/AOA
Any AOA beyond CLMAX results in a stall and lift drops off rapidly
Stall Characteristics
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall at the wing root and progress out to the wing tips
Aileron effectiveness is maintained at the wingtips, maintaining control
Various designs can be used to accomplish this:
Twisting the wing to create a lower angle of attack at the wing tip compared to the wing root
Adding strips to the first 20-25% of the leading edge to induce a stall earlier than otherwise
There’s More than One Way to Exceed the Critical AOA
If at ANY time the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Low Speed
As airspeed decreases, the AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
At a slow enough speed, the critical AOA is exceeded
High Speed
If an aircraft is in a high-speed dive and the pilot pulls back sharply on the elevator
Although the nose is raised, the aircraft continues downward for some amount of time
AOA changes from low to very high while the flight path remains the same
The aircraft reaches the critical AOA at a speed much higher than the published stall speed
Turns
The stall speed of an aircraft is higher in a level turn than in straight-and-level flight
In a turn, AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
If during the turn the AOA becomes excessive, the aircraft will stall
Various Factors and their Effect on Stall Speed 					AI.X.D.K2
A stall can occur at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting, depending on the total factors affecting the aircraft
Airspeed & Power Settings
Low Speed and/or Low Power Setting
Same as above
High Speed and/or High-Power Setting
Same as above
Additionally, in low wing planes, high power settings may reduce stall speed and increase lift
Propeller airflow over the wing roots can provide some lift even if the wing is stalled
Yaw Effects
Increased power at slow airspeeds and high angles of attack results in increased left turning tendencies - Anticipate considerable right rudder to maintain coordination
Torque Reaction – Based on Newton’s 3rd Law
The engine parts/propeller rotate right, an equal force attempts to rotate the plane left
In Flight: Left rolling tendency
On the Ground: Left turning  tendency
Corrected by offsetting the engine, aileron trim tabs, and/or aileron and rudder use
Corkscrew/Slipstream Effect
Corkscrewing propeller air strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer - pushes nose left
Strongest at high prop speeds/low forward speeds
Gyroscopic Action
Precession - Any force takes effect 90o ahead of, and in the direction of rotation
Pitch results in a yawing moment and vice versa
Correct with rudder/elevator
Asymmetric Loading (P Factor)
At high AOAs, the bite of the down moving blade is greater than the up moving blade
The center of thrust moves to the right of the propeller disc, causing a yaw to the left
Correct with right rudder
Configuration (Gear & Flaps)
Flaps - Reduce the stall speed of an aircraft
Most flaps increase the camber of the wing and change the chord line, producing more lift
Note the differing speeds on the airspeed indicator (green arc vs white arc)
Gear
The effects of gear can vary based on the aircraft design and characteristics
Gear extension increases drag and if not properly compensated for could lead to a stall
Weight - As the weight of the aircraft increases, the stall speed increases
The greater the weight, the greater the lift required, and therefore the higher AOA
Closer to the critical angle of attack
A lighter aircraft will stall at a slower airspeed (opposite of a heavy aircraft)
Center of Gravity
Forward CG
“Heavier,” and consequently slower
More nose-up elevator is required to maintain altitude
Tail must produce a greater down load resulting in greater wing loading
Added wing loading requires increased lift to maintain altitude
Higher Stall Speed
Higher AOA results in more induced drag and a higher stall speed (like heavy aircraft)
More Controllable in a Stall/Spin
More controllable than aft loaded aircraft
Due to the longer arm from elevator to CG
Additionally, the farther forward the CG, the greater the tendency for the nose to pitch down
Aft Loaded Aircraft
“Lighter,” and consequently faster
Less nose-up pressure required
Lower nose requires less down load
Decreased down load reduces wing loading, decreasing lift required to maintain altitude
Lower Stall Speed
Lower AOA results in less induced drag allowing for a faster cruise speed & lower stall speed
Less Controllable in a Stall/Spin
Recovery from a stall becomes progressively more difficult as the CG moves aft
The arm from the CG to the elevator is shortened
Additionally, the farther aft the CG, the less tendency for the nose to pitch down on its own
Load Factor
Any increase in the load factor increases the stall speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Pulling out of a steep descent, steep turns, aggressive control inputs, etc.
Bank Angle & Load Factor
Increased load factors are a characteristic of all banked turns
Tremendous loads are imposed on an airplane at bank angles above 45o
Snow, Ice, & Frost
Increase the stall speed
Disrupt smooth airflow over the wing causing the boundary layer to separate at an AOA lower than the critical AOA
To make matters worse, as ice accumulates weight is increased
More lift is required due to the added weight, but less lift is available due to the ice
As little as .8 millimeters of ice on the upper wing increases drag and reduces lift by 25%
RM: Power-On Stall Situations 							AI.X.D.K4, AI.X.D.R1
High power, high pitch situations
Generally associated with takeoff, climb & go-arounds. Most hazardous of these situations are likely:
Short field takeoff – high pitch, VX climb – closer to the stall speed
Go Around – changing configuration, pitch, power. Significant nose up trim, and distractions
Improper airspeed control in high power, high pitch, or similar situations
RM: Stall Warning Range & Limitations 		 					AI.X.D.R2
Buffet: Tends to occur prior to the stall horn
May not always occur (Ex: Cross controlled stalls can occur with little to no warning)
Stall Horn: Designed to provide warning of an approaching stall and time for stall recovery
Per 23.207
Must be a clear & distinct stall warning with flaps and gear in any normal position
Warning must begin at least 5 knots above stall speed and continue until the stall occurs
Must provide the pilot time to take action to avert the stall
Operational Ranges & Limitations: Vary between aircraft
Reference the POH for specific information
Ex: Uncoordinated flight may inhibit airflow at the indicator
Power-On Stalls 										AI.X.D.K1
Differences: Considerably louder and steeper than a power-off stall
Entry
Pre-Maneuver Checklist; Clear the area
Select an altitude - Must recover prior to 1,500’ AGL
Takeoff configuration (can be practiced clean as well)
Note the heading (bug the heading)
Getting into the Straight-Ahead Stall
Reduce power to slow to normal lift off speed while maintaining altitude
Visually - Nose pitches above the horizon; use a cloud, or other high visual reference
At VR, increase to takeoff power and maintain the specified climb attitude
Counter left turning tendencies with right rudder
As speed decreases & controls lose effectiveness, increase back pressure and right rudder
Visual references are primary, but back them up with the instruments
Use smooth movements to control the aircraft, nothing jerky
Getting into the Turning Stall
Same as a straight stall, except a specific bank is maintained (15-20o - Airplane Flying Handbook)
Apply power & pitch for the climb, and then establish the desired bank angle
Continually adjust aileron pressure to maintain bank
Reduced airspeed / control effectiveness
Overbanking tendency requires opposite aileron
Maintain coordination
Especially important in a turning, power-on stall due to the increased chance of a spin
Recognizing the Stall 										AI.X.D.K3
Announce the stages of the stall: Stall Warning Horn, Reduced Control Effectiveness, Buffet, Stall
Sight: Nose high attitude (especially high in a power on stall)
Sound: Stall warning horn, reduced RPM due to propeller load, slowing airspeed / airflow
Feel: Mushy / less effective controls, leaning back, buffeting and vibrations just before stall
Kinesthesia (sensing of movements by feel, “seat of the pants,” your “spidey sense”)
Experience based. When properly developed you can recognize when something doesn’t feel right
Aircraft Specific: Note any aircraft specific designs, indicators, characteristics, etc.
RM: Recovery - Disconnect, Pitch, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize, Configure 		AI.X.D.K5, AI.X.D.R4
Perform each step as appropriate
Disconnect the autopilot
Pitch nose down – Pitch attitude must be decreased immediately
Roll wings level – Regain / maintain directional control with coordinated aileron and rudder
Thrust/power as necessary – Stalls can occur at high/low power & airspeeds, adjust as required
In general, in a power-on stall, verify maximum power is set
Stabilize/establish the desired flight path – Establish a climb at the desired airspeed VY (or VX)
Once the stall is broken, do not aggressively lift the nose to reestablish a climb
Use smooth, controlled inputs and monitor the performance to ensure it is ready to climb
Configure – Once in a climb, configure as required (same flap and gear retraction as a go around)
Ailerons and Recovery
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall progressively outward from the wing root
Aileron control is maintained at high AOAs, providing more stable stall characteristics
During recovery, the return of lift begins at the tips and progresses towards the roots
Ailerons can be used to level the wings
If the wing is fully stalled (ailerons included), using ailerons can aggravate the stall
Attempting to raise the low (stalled) wing increases its AOA, further stalling the wing
Rudder and Recovery
The primary cause of spins is exceeding the critical AOA with improper rudder (uncoordinated flight)
Maintaining directional control / coordinated flight with rudder is vital in avoiding a spin
Common Errors (AFH 5-21)									AI.X.D.K6
Failure to adequately clear the area
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery
Inability to recognize an impending stall condition
Failure to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls, or recovering too early on a full stall
Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls
Failure to maintain proper coordination with the rudder throughout the stall and recovery
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped, prior to reducing AOA
Recovery is attempted without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA
Excessive forward pressure or not holding nose down controls until the stall warning is eliminated
Pilot attempts to level the wings and/or recover with power before reducing AOA
Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated
Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on entry, & inadvertent secondary stall during recovery
Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery
Losing situational awareness and failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions
RM: Hazards
Stall Warning during Normal Operation 							AI.X.D.R3
Recover!
The first thought is not how and why is this happening, the first reaction is to recover/fix the problem
When safe, then you can figure out how it happened
Secondary Stalls 										AI.X.D.R5
Occurs after recovery from a preceding stall
Pilot does not sufficiently reduce AOA or attempts to recover using only pitch or power
Perform the stall recovery procedure again, but do it right
Mitigation: Practice & perform proper recovery procedures (Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize)
Accelerated Stalls 										AI.X.D.R5
Higher G loads increase the stall speed (Ex. Steep turns, aggressive pull up)
Recover at the first indication of a stall
Push, roll, thrust, stabilize
Often, just removing the back pressure will break the stall
Mitigation: Use smooth control pressures
Elevator Trim Stalls 										AI.X.D.R5
Result of adding full power for a go-around with nose-up trim without maintaining control
Recover
Push - Regain control of the pitch attitude
Rough trim the airplane (fine tune later) to remove the excessive nose up pitch
Roll, Thrust, Stabilize as necessary
Once safe/under control, continue the go-around
Preventing Elevator Trim Stalls
Use smooth power applications
Anticipate and overcome the trim forces pitching the nose up, and maintain positive control
Cross-Controlled Stalls 									AI.X.D.R5
Aileron and rudder in opposite directions can lead to a cross-controlled stall
Most common in the traffic pattern
May have little to no warning of the impending stall
Release the crossed-controls and recover: Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Mitigation: Maintain coordination
Environmental Elements 								 	AI.X.D.R6
Turbulence
Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs to maintain altitude can exceed the critical AOA
In moderate/severe turbulence/strong crosswinds, use a higher-than-normal approach speed
When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence & speed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall
Microbursts
Can induce wind speeds greater than 100 knots and downdrafts as strong as 6,000 fpm
Depending on strength, climb ability can be minimized, if not eliminated
Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact
Can quickly lead to a stall making the problem far worse than it already is
If ground contact becomes a concern, increase pitch to minimize sink while avoiding a stall
Do not fly in or around thunderstorms or heavy rain showers where microbursts are most common
The best risk mitigation starts with effective planning
In the case of a microburst follow the POH procedures
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
See Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for details on recognizing/avoiding microbursts, and strategies for escape
High Density Altitude
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Collision Hazards 										AI.X.D.R7
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons/property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Antenna Towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally from the structure
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, & Task Management 					AI.X.D.R8
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Sterile cockpit procedures
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

Steep turns

Accelerated Stalls										AI.X.E.K1

Never practice accelerated stalls with flaps extended due to the lower design G-load limitations
Performing
Two methods for performing an accelerated stall per the Airplane Flying Handbook
Below VA, roll into 45o of bank & smoothly increase back pressure to induce a stall (most common)
Roll into a 45o bank above VA, and after the airspeed reaches VA, increase back pressure
Establish the desired flight attitude
At or Below VA (at this speed the airplane will stall before the limit load factor can be exceeded)
From straight and level, roll into a steep, level turn (About 45o)
Smoothly, firmly, and progressively increase the AOA until a stall occurs (at/below VA)
Increases wing loading, decreases airspeed, & the centrifugal force will push the pilot into the seat
Recognizing the Stall 										AI.X.E.K3
Buffet & Stall Warning Horn – Indicate an impending stall
The nose high attitude and noise reduction as the plane slows doesn’t occur in accelerated stalls
RM: Stall Warning Range & Limitations 		 					AI.X.E.R2
Buffet: Tends to occur prior to the stall horn
May not always occur (Ex: Cross controlled stalls can occur with little to no warning)
Stall Horn: Designed to provide warning of an approaching stall and time for stall recovery
Must be a clear & distinct stall warning with flaps and gear in any normal position
Warning must begin at least 5 knots above stall speed and continue until the stall occurs
Must provide the pilot time to take action to avert the stall
Operational Ranges & Limitations: Vary between aircraft
Reference the POH for specific information
Ex: Uncoordinated flight may inhibit airflow at the indicator
Characteristics

During a coordinated steep turn, the plane typically stalls exactly as it does from straight and level flight, except the buffet tends to be sharper and the pitching/rolling actions tend to be more sudden
Coordinated - Both wings stall simultaneously, just like straight and level
Slipping - Tends to roll rapidly toward the outside of the turn (Outside wing stalls 1st)
Skidding - Tends to roll rapidly toward the inside of the turn (Inside wing stalls 1st)
High or increasing descent rate
Note any aircraft specific indicators, characteristics, designs, etc.
RM: Recovery - Disconnect, Pitch, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize, Configure 		AI.X.E.K5, AI.X.E.R4
Perform each step as appropriate
Disconnect: the autopilot is likely already disconnected
Pitch: The elevator pressure should be released
Reduce the AOA and eliminate the stall warning
Roll: Use coordinated aileron and rudder pressures to level the wings
Thrust: Adjust power as necessary
If a high airspeed already exists, additional power may not be necessary
Power may even need to be reduced depending on the airspeed and attitude
If a spin were to develop, power should be taken to idle
Stabilize: Return to the desired flight path
Configure: Likely no changes applicable, but establish the desired configuration
Common Errors (AFH 5-21) 									AI.X.E.K6
Failure to adequately clear the area
Over-reliance on the airspeed indicator and slip-skid indicator while excluding other cues after recovery
Inability to recognize an impending stall condition
Failure to prevent a full stall during the conduct of impending stalls, or recovering too early on a full stall
Failure to maintain a constant bank angle during turning stalls
Failure to maintain proper coordination with the rudder throughout the stall and recovery
Not disconnecting the wing leveler or autopilot, if equipped, prior to reducing AOA
Recovery is attempted without recognizing the importance of pitch control and AOA
Not holding nose down controls until the stall warning is eliminated, or excessive forward pressure
Pilot attempts to level the wings and/or recover with power before reducing AOA
Failure to roll wings level after AOA reduction and stall warning is eliminated
Inadvertent accelerated stall by pulling too fast on entry, & inadvertent secondary stall during recovery
Excessive airspeed buildup during recovery
Losing situational awareness and failing to return to the desired flightpath or follow ATC instructions
RM: Hazards
Stall Warning during Normal Operation 							AI.X.E.R3
Recover!
The first thought is not how and why is this happening, the first reaction is to recover/fix the problem
When safe, then you can figure out how it happened
Secondary Stalls 										AI.X.E.R5
Occurs after recovery from a preceding stall
Pilot does not sufficiently reduce AOA or attempts to recover using only pitch or power
Perform the stall recovery procedure again, but do it right
Mitigation: Practice & perform proper recovery procedures (Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize)
Cross-Controlled Stalls 									AI.X.E.R5
Aileron and rudder in opposite directions can lead to a cross-controlled stall
Most common in the traffic pattern
May have little to no warning of the impending stall
Release the crossed-controls and recover: Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Mitigation: Maintain coordination
Spins 												AI.X.E.R5
Stall + Yaw (or uncoordinated flight)
In the case a spin develops, recover using PARE:
Power idle, Ailerons neutral, Rudder opposite the spin, Elevator forward
Once rotation stops, Rudder neutral, and elevator back pressure to raise the nose
Mitigation: Prevent a stall (recover at the first sign), in the case of a stall, maintain coordination
Environmental Elements 								 	AI.X.E.R6
Turbulence
Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs to maintain altitude can exceed the critical AOA
In moderate/severe turbulence/strong crosswinds, use a higher-than-normal approach speed
When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence & speed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall
Microbursts
Can induce wind speeds greater than 100 knots and downdrafts as strong as 6,000 fpm
Depending on strength, climb ability can be minimized, if not eliminated
Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact
Can quickly lead to a stall making the problem far worse than it already is
If ground contact becomes a concern, increase pitch to minimize sink while avoiding a stall
Do not fly in or around thunderstorms or heavy rain showers where microbursts are most common
The best risk mitigation starts with effective planning
In the case of a microburst follow the POH procedures
Aviation Weather Handbook (FAA-H-8083-28)
See Ch. 22 pgs. 7-18 for details on recognizing/avoiding microbursts, and strategies for escape
High Density Altitude
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa
How it affects Performance
As the air becomes less dense, it reduces:
Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils
Collision Hazards 										AI.X.E.R7
Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons/property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Antenna Towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally from the structure
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, & Task Management 					AI.X.E.R8
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Sterile cockpit procedures
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

X.E. Accelerated Stalls
Introduction
How
Accelerated Stall Aerodynamics 								AI.X.E.K2
A stall occurs when the smooth airflow over the wing is disrupted, and lift decreases rapidly
This happens when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack (AOA)
The critical AOA varies with aircraft, but is usually around 15-20o in GA aircraft
The Critical Angle of Attack/CLMAX
The point at which the airflow separates and there is a rapid reduction in lift is the stalling angle of attack, or the critical angle of attack, or CLMAX (the Maximum Coefficient of Lift)
CL = Coefficient of Lift
Measurement of lift as it relates to AOA
Determined by wind tunnel tests; based on airfoil design/AOA
Any AOA beyond CLMAX results in a stall and lift drops off rapidly
Stall Characteristics
Most general aviation aircraft are designed to stall at the wing root and progress out to the wing tips
Aileron effectiveness is maintained at the wingtips, maintaining control
Various designs can be used to accomplish this:
Twisting the wing to create a lower angle of attack at the wing tip compared to the wing root
Adding strips to the first 20-25% of the leading edge to induce a stall earlier than otherwise
What is an Accelerated Stall?
A plane will stall at speeds above the published stall speed when subject to load factors above 1G
Turning, pulling up, abrupt changes to the flight path
Stalls encountered anytime the load factor exceeds 1G are Accelerated Maneuver Stalls
Load Factor & Stall Speed
Load Factor: Ratio of the total load acting on the plane to the gross weight of the plane (G’s)
Any increase in the load factor increases the stall speed
Stall speed increases in proportion to the square root of the load factor
Pulling out of a steep descent, steep turns, aggressive control inputs, etc.
Bank Angle
Increased load factors are a characteristic of all banked turns
The wings must produce additional lift to maintain altitude (increased load factor)
Tremendous loads are imposed on an airplane at bank angles above 45o
Aggressive Pull ups and Load Factor
Can greatly increase G loading and quickly exceed the critical AOA
If an aircraft is in a high-speed dive and the pilot pulls back sharply on the elevator
Although the nose is raised, the aircraft continues downward for some amount of time
AOA changes from low to very high while the flight path remains the same
The aircraft reaches the critical AOA at a speed much higher than the published stall speed
Hazards of Accelerated Stalls
Significant load factor increases can be imposed when pulling out of steep dives or in steep turns
Can result in structural damage at high airspeeds
Stay below VA
Tend to occur at relatively high airspeeds and to be more aggressive due to the higher airspeeds
The aggressive stall, higher stall speed, and low pitch attitude can catch a pilot off guard
A prolonged accelerated stall may result in a spin or departure from controlled flight
Various Factors & their Effect on Stall Speed 						AI.X.E.K2
A stall can occur at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting, depending on the total factors affecting the aircraft
Airspeed & Power Settings
Low Speed and/or Low Power Setting
As airspeed decreases, the AOA must be increased to maintain altitude
At a slow enough speed, the critical AOA is exceeded
High Speed and/or High-Power Setting
If an aircraft is in a high-speed dive and the pilot pulls back sharply on the elevator
Although the nose is raised, the aircraft continues downward for some amount of time
AOA changes from low to very high while the flight path remains the same
The aircraft reaches the critical AOA at a speed much higher than the published stall speed
Additionally, in low wing planes, high power settings may reduce stall speed and increase lift
Propeller airflow over the wing roots can provide some lift even if the wing is stalled
Yaw Effects
Increased power at slow airspeeds and high angles of attack results in increased left turning tendencies - Anticipate considerable right rudder to maintain coordination
Torque Reaction – Based on Newton’s 3rd Law
The engine parts/propeller rotate right, an equal force attempts to rotate the plane left
In Flight: Left rolling tendency
On the Ground: Left turning tendency
Corrected by offsetting the engine, aileron trim tabs, and/or aileron and rudder use
Corkscrew/Slipstream Effect
Corkscrewing propeller air strikes the left side of the vertical stabilizer - pushes nose left
Strongest at high prop speeds/low forward speeds
Gyroscopic Action
Precession - Any force takes effect 90o ahead of, and in the direction of rotation
Pitch results in a yawing moment and vice versa
Correct with rudder/elevator
Asymmetric Loading (P Factor)
At high AOAs, the bite of the down moving blade is greater than the up moving blade
The center of thrust moves to the right of the propeller disc, causing a yaw to the left
Correct with right rudder
Configuration (Gear & Flaps)
Flaps - Reduce the stall speed of an aircraft
Most flaps increase the camber of the wing and change the chord line, producing more lift
Note the differing speeds on the airspeed indicator (green arc vs white arc)
Gear
The effects of gear can vary based on the aircraft design and characteristics
Gear extension increases drag and if not properly compensated for could lead to a stall
Weight - As the weight of the aircraft increases, the stall speed increases
The greater the weight, the greater the lift required, and therefore the higher AOA
Closer to the critical AOA
A lighter aircraft will stall at a slower airspeed (opposite of a heavy aircraft)
Center of Gravity (CG)
Forward CG
“Heavier” and consequently slower
More nose-up elevator is required to maintain altitude
Tail must produce a greater down load resulting in greater wing loading
Added wing loading requires increased lift to maintain altitude
Higher Stall Speed
Higher AOA results in more induced drag and a higher stall speed (like heavy aircraft)
More Controllable in a Stall/Spin
More controllable than aft loaded aircraft
Due to the longer arm from elevator to CG
Additionally, the farther forward the CG, the greater the tendency for the nose to pitch down
Aft Loaded Aircraft
“Lighter” and consequently faster
Less nose-up pressure required
Lower nose requires less down load
Decreased down load reduces wing loading, decreasing lift required to maintain altitude
Lower Stall Speed
Lower AOA results in less induced drag allowing for a faster cruise speed & lower stall speed
Less Controllable in a Stall/Spin
Recovery from a stall becomes progressively more difficult as the CG moves aft
The arm from the CG to the elevator is shortened
Additionally, the farther aft the CG, the less tendency for the nose to pitch down on its own
Snow, Ice, and Frost
Increase the stall speed
Disrupt smooth airflow over the wing causing the boundary layer to separate at an AOA lower than the critical AOA
To make matters worse, as ice accumulates weight is increased
More lift is required due to the added weight, but less lift is available due to the ice
As little as .8 millimeters of ice on the upper wing increases drag and reduces lift by 25%

Occurs after recovery from a preceding stall
Pilot does not sufficiently reduce AOA or attempts to recover using only pitch or power
Perform the stall recovery procedure again, but do it right
Mitigation: Practice & perform proper recovery procedures (Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize)

Aileron and rudder in opposite directions can lead to a cross-controlled stall
Most common in the traffic pattern
May have little to no warning of the impending stall
Release the crossed-controls and recover: Push, Roll, Thrust, Stabilize
Mitigation: Maintain coordination

Stall + Yaw (or uncoordinated flight)

Environmental Elements 								 	AI.X.E.R6
Turbulence
Can increase the stall speed
Sudden changes in relative wind, and/or aggressive control inputs to maintain altitude can exceed the critical AOA

When flying below minimum drag speed (L/DMAX) the aircraft exhibits speed instability
If disturbed by turbulence & speed decreases, drag increases, leading to further loss of speed
Total drag continues to rise, and airspeed continues to fall

Instinct can be to pitch excessively to counter the descent and avoid ground contact

High Density Altitude
Atmospheric Pressure
Since air is a gas, it can be compressed or expanded, affecting density
Air density affects performance - As density increases, performance increases & vice versa
What Changes Air Density (DA)? Barometric Pressure, Temperature, Altitude, and Humidity
Density varies directly with pressure - As pressure increases, density increases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with temperature – As temp increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with altitude - As altitude increases, density decreases & vice versa
Density varies inversely with humidity – As humidity increases, density decreases & vice versa

Power, since the engine takes in less air
Thrust, since the propeller is less efficient in thin air (less air is moved for every rotation)
Lift, because the thin air exerts less force on the airfoils

Collision Avoidance
Clearing Procedures
Climb/Descent: Use gentle banks to scan above/below the wings as well as other blind spots
Prior to any turn: Clear in the direction of the turn
Pre-Maneuver: Clearing turns – clear above/below, in front/behind
Clearly communicate intentions & location in practice areas
Scanning
Short, regularly spaced eye movements bringing successive areas into the central visual field
Each movement should not exceed 10o, each area should be observed for at least one second
Operation Lights On - Voluntary FAA safety program
Turn on landing lights during takeoff and when operating below 10,000’, day or night
Right-of-Way Rules (FAR 91.113)
An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other traffic
Converging Aircraft
Same Category Aircraft: The aircraft to the right has the right-of-way
Different Categories: Basically, the less maneuverable aircraft has the right-of-way
Balloons, gliders, and airships have the right of way over airplanes
An aircraft towing or refueling an aircraft has the right-of-way over engine driven aircraft
Approaching Head-on: Each pilot shall alter course to the right
Overtaking: Aircraft being overtaken has the right-of-way; when overtaking, pass on the right
Landing
Aircraft landing/on final to land have the right-of-way over those in flight or on the surface
When 2 or more aircraft are approaching for landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way
Don’t take advantage of either of these rules
Terrain
Study terminal charts and IFR/VFR chart altitudes, use Max Elevation Figures (MEFs)
Be extra vigilant at night, when terrain may be impossible to see until it is too late
Minimum Safe Altitudes (FAR 91.119)
Anywhere: Altitude allowing an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons/property
Congested Areas: 1,000’ above the highest obstacle within 2,000’
Other than Congested Areas: 500’ above the surface, except when over open water/sparsely populated areas, then no closer than 500’ to any person, vessel, vehicle, or structure
Obstacles & Wire Strike
Antenna Towers can reach over 1,000-2,000’ AGL
Most are supported by guy wires which can extend 1,500’ horizontally from the structure
Overhead Wires (may not be lit) span departures & landmarks pilots often follow
Lakes, highways, railroad tracks, etc.
Distractions, SA & Disorientation, & Task Management 					AI.X.E.R8
Distractions
They’re dangerous - Remove them from view or, if a person, explain the situation & ask them to stop
Focus on performance & clear for traffic - If distracted, recognize the problem, and fix it
Sterile cockpit procedures
Fly first! Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Situational awareness (SA) & Disorientation
Extremely important, lost SA has led to unsafe situations, mishaps, and incursions
Maintain SA
Starts with preflight planning
Know what’s coming next and stay ahead of the airplane
If SA is lost, admit it, and fix the problem
Disorientation can be caused by, or lead to, an upset
Push: Apply forward pressure to unload the plane
Roll: Roll aggressively to the nearest horizon
Thrust: Adjust as required
Stabilize: Return to a safe flight condition
Task Prioritization
Divide attention between the aircraft, scanning, and communicating (ATC or CTAF)
Understand what tasks need to be accomplished and when (use SOPs & checklists)
Recognize when you are getting behind and find a way to catch up
“Attack the closest alligator” – handle the most pressing problem and go from there
Proper task management can help prevent distractions, loss of SA, and disorientation
Safety is the number one priority – Aviate, Navigate, Communicate
Conclusion: Brief review of the main point

Introduction
How
Very interesting read on cross-controlled stalls from APS (Aviation Performance Solutions)
Cross-Controlled Stall Aerodynamics 						AI.X.F.K1, AI.X.F.K2
Situation
30o bank left turn to final with overshooting wind pushing you past the runway centerline
To avoid the overshoot, you add left rudder – aircraft rolls left, and the nose drops
Compensate with right aileron (crossed controls) and raising the nose
Still overshooting so you add more left rudder (more right aileron and back pressure to counter)
Suddenly, the aircraft rolls sharply left, inverted (or even into a spin)
Instinct is to recover with more right aileron and back elevator pressure
Aircraft rolls further left and accelerates the descent to the ground
Why did this happen?
A cross-controlled stall occurs when the critical AOA is exceeded with aileron pressure applied in one direction and rudder pressure in the opposite direction
Using rudder to turn requires opposite (right) aileron and back pressure to maintain bank / altitude
Opposite Aileron
As the right wing accelerates, right aileron is necessary to maintain the bank angle
Right aileron increases the AOA on the left wing, and decreases it on the right
The inside, low wing, has a higher AOA than the outside, high wing
Back Elevator Pressure (leads to the stall)
The nose drop, due to increasing drag, leads to increased back pressure to maintain altitude
Increased back pressure to maintain the same flight path leads to increased AOA
Overall
AOA of the left, inside wing, is increased with right aileron
AOA of both wings is increased with the added back pressure
The Stall and the Reaction to the Stall
At the point of the stall, the inside wing has a higher AOA and therefore stalls first
The plane rolls in the direction of the low wing (often inverted if not corrected quickly)
If you attempt to roll wings level (with right aileron), it further increases AOA on the inside wing
With the ground approaching rapidly, instinct is to pull up, making the stall even deeper
Stall + Yaw = Spin. You could very easily end up in a low altitude spin
The Moral of the Story
Stay coordinated, especially low to the ground
Instinctual reactions will aggravate the situation
In the case of an overshoot, or a cross controlled situation, go around and avoid the risk

Understand conditions that lead to a cross-controlled stall: Opposite, uncoordinated aileron/rudder
